lesson:sections/soft-skills/lessons/the-.note:
Ive noticed this in my day job. For example when it comes to gathering requirements to solve internal issues or trying to fix problems in a team people can be reluctant to show their real sentiments, needs, etc. Sometimes its because of how the context makes the feel or because they are in conflict with some of their other needs.

Psychological safety, politics, incentives, ego, etc.

I think i tend to put my expertise in my action. I try hard to level my language so that its appropriate for my audience or for what I'm trying to accomplish. I agree that jargon and domain specific terminology can sometimes disorient people, especially when they're not actually in the weeds.
lesson:sections/soft-skills/lessons/the-.quote: visible expertise can make clients guarded, because credentials and gadgets raise their sense of being judged or of being behind. Setting the trappings aside, being curious, and putting the client's intelligence and situation first, lowers the barriers.
lesson:sections/soft-skills/lessons/the-.title: The Trusted Advisor: Earning Client Trust

lesson:sections/soft-skills/lessons/the-.note:
Next client conversation, I will:
  1. Note what the client feels: Name the feeling (and your own, carefully).
  2. Relax your mind before the meeting: Clear distractions; remind yourself it is about the client.
  3. Listen to everything: Paraphrase what you hear until you can say it back.
